newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Washington sees hope for China WTO accord - Sasser.
newsitem.headline: Washington sees hope for China WTO accord - Sasser.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador to China James Sasser said on Friday Washington hoped to conclude talks on China's entry into the World Trade Organisation by the time Beijing's top leader visits the White House later this year.
"There is hope that could be concluded in time for President Jiang Zemin's visit this fall to the United States," Sasser told a business luncheon in Hong Kong.
"I think there is hope. Realistically, it's going to be difficult to do, but not impossible."
Sasser also predicted a tough debate over renewal of China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status this year, but he was optimistic it would be granted.
Sasser said Washington would continue to push vigorously to try to reach a WTO agreement with China in conjunction with other members of the global trade body.

Jiang is expected to visit the United States later this year for a proposed summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton. Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen's visit to Washington next week is expected to lay the ground for the summit meeting.
Demands that China improve market access have delayed Beijing's entry into the WTO.
Numerous issues remain to be resolved on China's decade-long entry application to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and its successor organisation, the WTO, diplomats said.

They cite a need for Beijing to scrap a wide range of trade barriers, while opening markets in agriculture, financial services, trading rights and distribution systems, and clarifying controversial subsidies to state-run industries.

As for China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status, which usually arouses fierce congressional debate when it comes up for annual review in June, Sasser said the White House would face an uphill battle to renew it again this year.
"I predict they will be successful. But I also predict this is going to be a difficult battle," he added.

Sasser added that Beijing "still has much to do in terms of protecting freedom of political and religious expression" and told his audience that business leaders had a role to play in promoting human rights in China.

"As Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright said recently, our many interests in China reinforce one another -- 'they cannot be separated into discrete boxes'. Human rights and business interests are complementary, not contradictory."
Sasser warned China to respect human rights in Hong Kong, which will come under Beijing control on July 1, or stand to lose billions of dollars of investment from the United States.
He also said the U.S. government would closely watch Hong Kong after it reverts to Chinese rule in 67 days.
"Americans have invested $15 billion here. To sustain this U.S. presence requires a society governed by the rule of law and protection of basic freedom," he said.
In a separate development on Friday, the United States said it would grant 10-year multiple-entry visas to holders of new Hong Kong passports after China takes the territory back from Britain.
